facts: Its Hebrew name is simply its first word, Bereshit, "In the beginning".
Fifty chapters cover more time than the rest of the Bible put together, from creation to a coffin in Egypt.
Every later book assumes you know this one: the flood, Abraham, Jacob's twelve sons, Joseph.

1.title: Creation
1.note: Seven days, and a refrain: "God saw that it was good", seven times over, until the seventh says "very good". Notice that light is made on day one and the sun not until day four. The order is a poem before it is a timetable.

3.title: The fall
3.note: The serpent's first words are a question, and the first lie in the Bible is a promise. Watch for the three consequences and the one strange mercy: God makes them clothes before sending them out.

22.title: Abraham and Isaac
22.note: The word "love" appears here for the first time in the Bible, and it is a father's for his son. Read verse 8 twice. The place, Moriah, is where the Temple will later stand.

37.title: Joseph sold
37.note: The coat, the dreams, the pit, and a price of twenty pieces of silver. Everything in the last fourteen chapters of Genesis turns on what his brothers do here, and on what Joseph does with it.

2.t: Man and Woman in the Garden

Exodus.eyebrow: The way out. A people is made.
facts: Its name is Greek for "going out". The Hebrew name is "Names", after its first words.
Half the book is a journey and half is a building: the second half is instructions for the tabernacle, twice over.
It contains the Passover, the Ten Commandments and the golden calf, all within forty chapters.

3.title: The burning bush
3.note: God gives his name, and it is a verb: "I AM WHO I AM". Moses offers four excuses in two chapters. Watch how each is answered with a sign rather than an argument.

14.title: The sea
14.note: The crossing itself takes a few verses. The chapter is mostly fear, and the line that answers it: "Yahweh will fight for you, and you shall be still." The song in the next chapter is one of the oldest texts in the Bible.

20.title: The Ten Commandments
20.note: Ten sayings, given twice in the Bible, here and in Deuteronomy 5. The first four are about God and the last six about neighbours. The people ask Moses to speak instead, because the voice is too much.

facts: It is the book of the priests, the Levites, and most of it is instruction rather than story.
It sits at the exact centre of the Torah, and its own centre is chapter 16, the Day of Atonement.
Jesus quotes it for the second greatest commandment: "love your neighbor as yourself", from 19:18.

16.title: The Day of Atonement
16.note: Two goats: one is offered, the other carries the sins of the people out into the wilderness. That second one is where the word "scapegoat" comes from. This is the one day a year the high priest enters the innermost room.

19.title: Be holy
19.note: The chapter Jesus reached for. Leaving the edge of your field for the poor, honest weights, not holding a grudge, and in verse 18, love your neighbour as yourself. Holiness here is mostly about how you treat people.

8.t: Moses Consecrates Aaron and His Sons

10.t: The Sin of Nadab and Abihu

facts: Named for its two censuses, one at the start and one at the end, a generation apart.
Its Hebrew name is "In the wilderness", which is a better description of what happens.
The oldest surviving words of any Bible text are from this book: the priestly blessing, on two silver scrolls from before the exile.

6.title: The blessing
6.note: Verses 24 to 26 are the oldest biblical text ever found, scratched onto two tiny silver amulets buried outside Jerusalem before the exile. They are still said over congregations every week.

13.title: The spies
13.note: Twelve men go in, ten come back afraid. This is the chapter that costs a generation forty years. Only Caleb and Joshua say the land can be taken, and only they will live to enter it.

22.title: Balaam's donkey
22.note: A prophet hired to curse Israel is stopped by his own donkey, who sees the angel he cannot. The animal speaks; the prophet argues with it. Balaam ends up blessing the people four times.

4.t: The Numbering of the Levite Clans

facts: The name means "second law": Moses retells the story and the commandments to the generation about to cross over.
It is the book Jesus quotes most when tempted in the wilderness, all three answers come from it.
It ends with Moses seeing the land from a mountain and dying without entering it.

6.title: Hear, O Israel
6.note: Verse 4 is the Shema, the prayer observant Jews say morning and evening: "Yahweh our God, Yahweh is one." Verse 5 is the commandment Jesus called the greatest. Teach them to your children, when you sit and when you walk.

34.title: The death of Moses
34.note: He sees the whole land from Mount Nebo and is told he will not cross into it. He is buried by God, and no one knows where. "There has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses."

facts: Joshua's name is the same as Jesus' in Hebrew: Yeshua, "Yahweh saves".
The book is half conquest and half a survey: chapters of boundaries, town by town.
It ends with a choice put to the people at Shechem: "choose this day whom you will serve".

6.title: Jericho
6.note: Seven days, seven priests, seven trumpets, and on the seventh day seven circuits. No siege, only walking and a shout. Rahab, who hid the spies, is spared, and she appears again in the family tree of Jesus.

facts: A cycle repeats a dozen times: the people forget, are oppressed, cry out, and a deliverer is raised.
The judges are not lawyers. Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah and Samson are warriors, and flawed ones.
Its last line explains everything before it: "there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes."

16.title: Samson and Delilah
16.note: The strongest man in the Bible is undone not by an army but by being asked the same question four times. Blinded and grinding grain in Gaza, he prays once, and brings the house down.

The Failure to Complete the Conquest

facts: It is set in the time of the Judges and reads like a breath of clean air after them.
Ruth is a Moabite, a foreigner, and the book ends by naming her as King David's great-grandmother.
It is read aloud in synagogues at the harvest feast of Shavuot, because it is a harvest story.

1.title: Where you go, I will go
1.note: Naomi has lost her husband and both sons. She tells her daughters-in-law to go home, and one does. Ruth's answer in verses 16 and 17 is one of the most quoted vows in the Bible, and it is made to a mother-in-law.

facts: Three lives run through it: Samuel the last judge, Saul the first king, and David waiting in the wings.
The two books of Samuel were one scroll; they were split because it was too long to handle.
Saul is chosen for being tall and loses everything for being impatient. David is chosen for his heart.

3.title: Speak, your servant is listening
3.note: A boy hears his name in the night and thinks it is the old priest calling. Three times. Eli, who has not heard from God in years, is the one who works out who is speaking.

17.title: David and Goliath
17.note: Notice how long the chapter spends on the giant's armour, and how little on the fight. Five smooth stones, one used. David's speech before the throw is the point: "the battle is Yahweh's".

2.t: A Prophecy against the House of Eli

facts: It is one man's reign, from his anointing in Hebron to his old age, victories and disasters together.
The Bible does not protect David. His worst act and its consequences take up half the book.
Chapter 7's promise to David is the root of every later hope for a Messiah, an anointed king from his line.

7.title: A house for David
7.note: David wants to build God a house. God answers with a play on the word: he will build David a house, a dynasty, and a son of David will reign forever. Every Gospel opens by tracing Jesus to this promise.

12.title: You are the man
12.note: Nathan tells the king a story about a rich man who steals a poor man's one lamb. David is furious, and then the prophet says four words. David's repentance is Psalm 51.

facts: It opens with the Temple being built and ends with the kingdom torn in two, north and south.
The prophet Elijah appears without introduction in chapter 17 and dominates the rest.
Kings is judged by one standard throughout: did the king lead the people toward God or away.

3.title: Solomon's wisdom
3.note: Offered anything, the young king asks for a listening heart. The test comes at once: two women, one living baby, and a sword. The whole nation hears the verdict and knows what kind of king it has.

18.title: Carmel
18.note: One prophet against four hundred and fifty. They shout all day; Elijah mocks them, then rebuilds the altar with twelve stones, soaks it three times, and prays a sentence. Fire falls.

19.title: The still small voice
19.note: The day after his greatest victory, Elijah runs for his life and asks to die. God feeds him, walks him to a mountain, and speaks: not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in a whisper.

facts: Elisha takes Elijah's cloak in chapter 2 and performs twice as many miracles as his master.
The northern kingdom falls to Assyria in chapter 17; the southern falls to Babylon in chapter 25.
It ends with the Temple burned and the king of Judah eating at Babylon's table. The next word is Chronicles, starting again from Adam.

2.title: The chariot of fire
2.note: Elijah is taken up in a whirlwind while Elisha watches, and the cloak falls. Elisha asks for a double share of his spirit, the inheritance of a firstborn son, and strikes the Jordan with the cloak to see if he got it.

25.title: Jerusalem falls
25.note: The city starves, the wall is broken, the Temple is burned, and the bronze pillars are carried off in pieces. This is the exile the prophets warned of. The book's last verses are a small mercy shown to a captive king.

facts: The first nine chapters are genealogies, from Adam to the return from exile, the longest family tree in the Bible.
It retells David's reign from Samuel, leaving out Bathsheba and Absalom, and adding the plans for the Temple.
It was written after the exile, for people asking whether the old promises still held.

16.title: The ark comes home
16.note: David brings the ark into Jerusalem and appoints singers for the first time. The psalm he gives them in this chapter is stitched from Psalms 105, 96 and 106. Worship with music begins here.

3.t: The Royal Line After the Exile

2 Chronicles.eyebrow: From the Temple to its ashes.
facts: It follows only the southern kings, Judah, and measures each by his care for the Temple.
In the Hebrew Bible this is the last book, so the whole Old Testament ends on its final word: "go up".
Its closing verses, Cyrus sending the exiles home, are repeated word for word to open Ezra.

36.title: Cyrus
36.note: Seventy years of exile, and then a Persian emperor is moved to send the people home and rebuild. Isaiah had named Cyrus more than a century earlier. In the Hebrew Bible these are the Old Testament's last words.

facts: Ezra and Nehemiah were one book, the story of two returns from Babylon fifty years apart.
It opens with the decree of Cyrus and the first exiles carrying the Temple vessels back.
Ezra himself does not appear until chapter 7. He is a scribe, and his subject is the Law.

3.title: The foundation laid
3.note: When the new Temple's foundation is set, the young shout for joy and the old, who remember the first one, weep aloud. Verse 13 says no one could tell the two sounds apart.

6.t: The Returned Exiles Keep the Passover

8.t: The Exiles Who Returned with Ezra

facts: Nehemiah is the king's cupbearer in Persia, and asks leave to go and rebuild Jerusalem's walls.
Much of the book is his own memoir, in the first person, including his prayers.
The builders work with a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other, and finish in fifty-two days.

8.title: Ezra reads the Law
8.note: The whole people stand from dawn to noon while the Law is read aloud and explained, and they weep at what they hear. They are told not to: "the joy of Yahweh is your strength."

12.t: The Priests and Levites Who Returned

Tobit.eyebrow: A journey, an angel, a fish.
facts: A short novel set among exiles in Nineveh: a blind father, a son sent on a journey, and a bride under a curse.
The travelling companion is the angel Raphael in disguise. His name means "God heals".
Fragments of it in Hebrew and Aramaic were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls.

6.title: The fish
6.note: A fish leaps from the Tigris at Tobias, and his companion tells him to keep its heart, liver and gall. Every one of them will be needed. The dog that follows them is one of the few pets in the Bible.

12.title: I am Raphael
12.note: The guide will take no payment and, having seen the family reunited and healed, tells them who he is: one of the seven who stand before God. Then he is gone, and they write it all down.

facts: Her name simply means "Jewish woman". She stands for the whole people.
The enemy general Holofernes has the strongest army in the world, and loses to one woman with a plan.
The book's history is deliberately impossible, Nebuchadnezzar ruling Assyria, which is a way of saying this is a parable.

13.title: The tent
13.note: Alone with the drunk general, Judith prays twice, takes his own sword, and strikes twice. She walks out through the enemy camp with his head in a bag, and the city's gates open to her at dawn.

Esther.eyebrow: For such a time as this.
facts: In the Hebrew text, God is never named. Not once. The Greek additions at the end of this book are where the prayers are.
It explains the feast of Purim, still kept with the reading of this scroll and much noise at Haman's name.
Chapters 11 to 16 here are the Greek additions, printed after the Hebrew book so nothing in it moves.

4.title: For such a time as this
4.note: Mordecai's message to the queen, verse 14, is the hinge of the book: if you stay silent, help will come from elsewhere, but who knows whether you were made queen for this. Her answer: "if I perish, I perish".

14.title: Esther's prayer
14.note: This chapter is from the Greek text, and it gives Esther what the Hebrew never does: a voice to God. She takes off the crown, covers her head in ashes, and prays before going in to the king.

facts: A Greek king outlaws the Jewish faith and sets up an idol in the Temple. A priest and his five sons fight back.
It is the origin of Hanukkah: the retaking and rededication of the Temple in chapter 4.
Written in Hebrew, it survives only in Greek. It reads like Samuel and Kings, on purpose.

2.title: Mattathias
2.note: An old priest in a small town is ordered to sacrifice to an idol. He refuses, kills the man who complies, and flees to the hills with his sons. His dying speech names the heroes of the whole Old Testament.

4.title: The Temple retaken
4.note: Judas Maccabeus, "the hammer", clears the Temple, builds a new altar from uncut stones, and dedicates it for eight days. Verse 59 makes the anniversary a feast. It is still kept: Hanukkah.

2 Maccabees.eyebrow: The same war, seen from heaven.
facts: Not a sequel. It retells the start of the same revolt, condensed by its own account from a five-volume history now lost.
It is where the Bible speaks most plainly of resurrection, of praying for the dead, and of martyrdom.
Its author admits the work was hard: "sweat and loss of sleep", he says, and asks the reader's indulgence.

7.title: The seven brothers
7.note: Seven sons are tortured to death one by one in front of their mother for refusing to eat pork, and each dies speaking of resurrection. The mother, who watches all seven, dies last. Read what she says to the youngest.

12.title: Prayer for the dead
12.note: After a battle, Judas finds idols on his own fallen soldiers. He takes a collection and sends it to Jerusalem for a sacrifice on their behalf, "that they might be delivered from their sin". This is where prayer for the dead has its roots.

facts: Job is not an Israelite, and the book never mentions the Law, the covenant or the Temple. Its question is everyone's.
Two chapters of story frame forty of poetry: three friends, a young man, and finally God, out of a storm.
The friends say suffering is deserved. The book's last word is that they were wrong.

1.title: Have you considered my servant Job?
1.note: A wager in heaven the man on earth never hears about. He loses everything in four messages, each arriving before the last has finished. His answer is a sentence: "Yahweh gave, and Yahweh has taken away."

38.title: Out of the whirlwind
38.note: After thirty-five chapters of argument, God speaks, and asks questions. Where were you when I laid the earth's foundations? Have you walked the springs of the sea? Not one of Job's questions is answered. All of them are outgrown.

42.title: The end of Job
42.note: Job gets double what he lost, and three new daughters, who are named, which his sons are not, and given an inheritance alongside their brothers, which daughters were not. God rebukes the friends and tells Job to pray for them.

facts: One hundred and fifty poems, in five books, each ending with a doxology. Half carry David's name.
Every mood is here: praise, fury, despair, thanksgiving, and the wish that your enemy's children come to harm.
It is the book the New Testament quotes most, and the one Jesus prayed from on the cross.

1.title: The two ways
1.note: The gate to the whole book. Two paths, a tree by water and chaff in the wind. It never mentions prayer or the Temple, only a person who takes delight in the Law and thinks about it day and night.

22.title: My God, why have you forsaken me?
22.note: Jesus prays its first line from the cross. Read on: pierced hands and feet, lots cast for clothing, and then, at verse 22, a turn to praise that does not stop. The Gospels assume you know the ending.

23.title: The Lord is my shepherd
23.note: Six verses, and the most known passage in the Bible. Notice the shift halfway: it starts by speaking about God, "he leads me", and at the darkest point turns to speak to him, "you are with me".

51.title: Have mercy on me
51.note: David's prayer after Nathan said "you are the man". No excuse, no bargain. "Create in me a clean heart" uses the verb for creation in Genesis 1, a thing only God does.

119.title: The longest chapter
119.note: One hundred and seventy-six verses, in twenty-two stanzas of eight, each stanza's lines beginning with the same Hebrew letter, in order. Almost every verse names the Law. It is the alphabet, spent on delight.

137.title: By the rivers of Babylon
137.note: The exiles are asked to sing for their captors and cannot. The psalm ends with a curse so violent that churches usually stop reading before it. The Bible does not; it keeps the anger, and gives it to God.

150.title: Let everything that has breath
150.note: The last psalm has no request in it at all. Thirteen times, "praise", and every instrument in the orchestra. The book that began with a man alone with the Law ends with everything alive, making noise.

facts: Sayings collected over centuries, most under Solomon's name, some from a king's mother and from unknown sages.
Its theme is set in the first chapter: "the fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge".
Wisdom is a woman here, calling in the streets, and she says she was beside God at the making of the world.

8.title: Wisdom speaks
8.note: Wisdom is not an idea here but a person, standing at the city gate. From verse 22 she describes the creation of the world as something she watched from beside God, "rejoicing always before him". The New Testament heard this and thought of Christ.

31.title: A capable wife
31.note: The book ends with a poem about a woman, an acrostic, twenty-two verses on the Hebrew alphabet. She trades, plants, manufactures and gives, and her husband is known at the gate because of her.

facts: The speaker calls himself Qoheleth, "the one who gathers", in the assembly or in thought.
Its refrain, "vanity of vanities", is the Hebrew hevel: breath, mist, a thing you cannot hold.
It is the most doubting book in the Bible, and the Bible kept it.

3.title: A time for everything
3.note: Fourteen pairs: born and die, plant and pluck up, weep and laugh, keep silence and speak. Then, in verse 11, that God has set eternity in the human heart, and made it impossible to see the whole.

facts: God is never named in it. It is two lovers speaking, and a chorus.
Jewish and Christian readers have heard in it God's love for his people, and it is read in full at Passover.
Its title means the best of songs, the way "holy of holies" means the holiest place.

8.title: Strong as death
8.note: Verses 6 and 7: love is as strong as death, its flashes are flashes of fire, and many waters cannot quench it. The lovers' last exchange is a request to hurry.

3.t: Solomon Arrives on His Wedding Day

facts: Written in Greek, probably in Alexandria, by a Jew steeped in philosophy, within a century of Jesus.
It is the Old Testament's clearest voice on immortality: the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God.
Its second half retells the Exodus as a meditation on how God treats the wise and the foolish.

2.title: Lying in wait for the righteous
2.note: The wicked reason it through: life is short, so take what you can, and the righteous man is an inconvenience. "Let us condemn him to a shameful death." Christians reading this saw the crucifixion described in advance.

3.title: The souls of the righteous
3.note: "In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died." This chapter is read at more funerals than almost any other. Its answer to death is not that it does not happen, but that it is not the end of the story.

facts: Also called Ecclesiasticus, "the church's book", because it was used so much for teaching converts.
We know the author: Jesus ben Sira of Jerusalem. His grandson translated it into Greek in Egypt and wrote a preface saying so.
It is the longest wisdom book, fifty-one chapters on friendship, money, speech, grief, doctors, and God.

24.title: Wisdom's own story
24.note: Wisdom speaks of coming from the mouth of God, seeking a home in every nation, and being told to settle in Israel. Then, in verse 23, the turn: all this is the Law of Moses. The Torah is Wisdom, made local.

44.title: Let us now praise famous men
44.note: The start of a roll call of Israel's heroes that runs to chapter 50, from Enoch to the high priest the author himself had watched. "Their bodies are buried in peace, but their name lives on."

facts: Sixty-six chapters, the longest prophetic book, spanning more than a century from Assyria to the return from Babylon.
The New Testament quotes it more than any other prophet: a child is born, a voice in the wilderness, the suffering servant.
A complete scroll of Isaiah, a thousand years older than any other known copy, was found in a cave near the Dead Sea in 1947.

6.title: Holy, holy, holy
6.note: The year the king dies, Isaiah sees the throne, the seraphim, and the smoke. A coal from the altar touches his mouth. Then the question, "whom shall I send?", and the answer that begins his life: "Here I am, send me."

40.title: Comfort my people
40.note: After thirty-nine chapters of judgment, a new voice: comfort. A voice in the wilderness, grass that withers, a shepherd carrying lambs, and eagles' wings. Handel opened the Messiah with its first line.

53.title: The suffering servant
53.note: A man despised, pierced for our transgressions, silent as a lamb, buried with the rich. Written centuries before the crucifixion, it is the chapter the first Christians reached for to explain it. Read Acts 8 afterward.

facts: Called as a boy, he spent forty years telling Jerusalem it would fall, and lived to watch it happen.
He was beaten, put in stocks, thrown into a cistern and carried off to Egypt against his will.
His scribe Baruch wrote the scroll; when the king burned it, Jeremiah dictated it again, longer.

1.title: Before I formed you
1.note: "I am only a child," he says. God touches his mouth and shows him two things: an almond branch, the first tree to wake in spring, and a boiling pot tipping from the north. The whole book is in those two pictures.

31.title: The new covenant
31.note: In the middle of the ruin, a promise: a new covenant, written not on stone but on hearts, and sins remembered no more. Verses 31 to 34 are the longest Old Testament passage quoted in the New, in Hebrews 8.

facts: Five poems over the ruins of Jerusalem, traditionally Jeremiah's, sitting in the ashes.
Four of the five are acrostics: the alphabet, in order, imposed on chaos. Chapter 3 goes through it three times.
It is read in full each year on the day the Temple's destruction is remembered.

3.title: New every morning
3.note: The darkest of the five poems, and at its exact centre, verses 22 and 23: his mercies do not fail, they are new every morning. The hope is not at the end. It is buried in the middle, where you have to dig for it.

facts: Baruch was Jeremiah's scribe. This book is set among the exiles in Babylon, sending words home.
Its heart is a poem on Wisdom, chapters 3 and 4, which ends by saying she appeared on earth and lived among people.
Chapter 6 here is a separate work, the Letter of Jeremiah, a long argument against idols.

3.title: Where is wisdom found?
3.note: Not with the giants, not with the merchants, not with the kings. Verse 37 says God found her and gave her to Israel, and then: "she appeared on earth and lived among men". Christians have read that line at Christmas.

6.title: The Letter of Jeremiah
6.note: A different book, joined here. Seventy-three verses on idols: they are gilded but rust, they cannot save themselves from fire or thieves, bats and birds sit on them. The refrain, ten times: they are not gods, do not fear them.

facts: A priest in exile, called by a vision of wheels and living creatures that has puzzled readers for 2,500 years.
He acted his prophecies out: lying on his side for months, shaving his head, refusing to mourn his wife.
The book ends with nine chapters measuring a Temple that was never built, and a city named "Yahweh is there".

1.title: The wheels
1.note: Four creatures with four faces, wheels within wheels full of eyes, a crystal floor, a throne, and on it a figure like fire. Ezekiel's word for all of it is careful: "the appearance of the likeness of the glory". He falls on his face.

37.title: The valley of dry bones
37.note: "Can these bones live?" The prophet is told to preach to a valley of skeletons, and they rattle together, grow flesh, and stand: a vast army. It is the exile's return, and it has been sung about ever since.

facts: Half stories, half visions. A Jewish boy rises in Babylon's court and outlasts three kings and two empires.
Two languages: it switches from Hebrew into Aramaic in chapter 2 and back in chapter 8.
Chapters 13 and 14 here, Susanna and Bel and the Dragon, are from the Greek text, and Susanna is the Bible's first detective story.

3.title: The fiery furnace
3.note: Three men refuse to bow to a golden statue and are thrown into a furnace heated seven times over. The king counts four figures walking in the fire. Their answer before the sentence is the point: our God can save us, and even if he does not, we will not bow.

6.title: The lions' den
6.note: Daniel is old now, and the law is written to catch him at prayer. The king who signs it cannot sleep. At dawn he runs to the pit and calls in, and the answer comes back.

13.title: Susanna
13.note: Two respected elders try to blackmail a woman into adultery and, refused, accuse her of it. She is condemned. A young Daniel stops the execution and questions the men separately: under which tree? Their answers do not match.

facts: God tells the prophet to marry a woman who will be unfaithful, and to take her back. The marriage is the message.
His children are named as warnings: "not pitied" and "not my people". Both names are reversed by the end.
It is the first of the twelve short prophets, one scroll in the Hebrew Bible, "the Book of the Twelve".

11.title: When Israel was a child
11.note: God as a parent: teaching a toddler to walk, lifting him to his cheek, bending down to feed him. Then the anger, and then, in verse 8, the anger failing: "how can I give you up?" Matthew quotes verse 1 of Jesus.

facts: It opens with a plague of locusts described so closely you can hear them, and treats it as an army from God.
Nothing in it dates it. Joel could be from almost any century of the kingdom.
Peter quoted it to explain Pentecost: "I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh".

2.title: I will pour out my Spirit
2.note: The locust army first, and then "rend your heart and not your garments". From verse 28 the promise Peter read aloud in Acts 2: sons and daughters prophesying, old men dreaming, young men seeing visions, everyone.

2.t: I Will Pour Out My Spirit

facts: Amos was a herdsman and fig-farmer from the south, sent north to preach in a prosperous kingdom's royal shrine.
His target is not idolatry first but injustice: the poor sold for a pair of sandals.
He was told to go home. His answer: "I was no prophet, nor a prophet's son", just a man God took from the flock.

5.title: Let justice roll down
5.note: God says he hates their festivals and will not listen to their songs. What he wants is in verse 24: justice rolling like water and righteousness like an unfailing stream. Martin Luther King Jr. quoted it at the Lincoln Memorial.

2.t: Judgment on Moab, Judah, and Israel

facts: The shortest book in the Old Testament, twenty-one verses, all aimed at Edom, Israel's cousin nation.
Edom descends from Esau, and stood by, or joined in, when Jerusalem fell. That is the grievance.
Nothing is known of Obadiah himself. The name means "servant of Yahweh".
Every other prophet's book is his words. Jonah's is his story, and he speaks only eight words of prophecy in it.
He runs the wrong way, is swallowed, preaches one sentence, converts a city, and sulks about it.
Jesus mentioned the fish: three days in it, as he would be three days in the earth.

4.title: The plant and the worm
4.note: Nineveh repents and Jonah is furious. God grows a plant to shade him, then sends a worm to kill it, and Jonah grieves for the plant. God's last question is the book's point: you pity a plant. Should I not pity a city?

4.t: Jonah’s Anger at the LORD’s Compassion

facts: A country prophet, contemporary with Isaiah, from a village in the hills.
He names Bethlehem as the birthplace of the coming ruler, the verse the scribes quoted to Herod.
Chapter 6, verse 8 is the whole Law in a sentence: do justice, love mercy, walk humbly with your God.

6.title: What does the Lord require?
6.note: God takes Israel to court and calls the mountains as witnesses. What is the charge? What is the fee? Thousands of rams, rivers of oil, a firstborn child? No. Verse 8. Three things, and none of them cost money.

4.t: The Mountain of the House of the LORD

facts: A century after Jonah, the same city gets no second chance. Nahum announces its destruction, and it fell in 612 BC.
Its poetry is vivid: chariots in the streets, the queen's maids moaning like doves, the palace dissolving.
His name means "comfort". The comfort is for Nineveh's victims.
The prophet argues with God, and God answers. Then he argues with the answer.
"The righteous shall live by his faith", 2:4, is quoted three times in the New Testament and launched the Reformation.
It ends with a psalm: though the fig tree does not blossom and the stalls are empty, yet I will rejoice.

2.title: The righteous shall live by faith
2.note: Habakkuk stations himself on the watchtower and waits for a reply. It comes: write the vision plainly, it will not lie, and if it delays, wait. Verse 4 is the line Paul built Romans and Galatians on.

facts: A prophet of royal blood, great-great-grandson of King Hezekiah, preaching in the reign of the reformer Josiah.
His opening threatens to sweep everything off the face of the earth. His ending has God singing.
The medieval hymn Dies Irae, "day of wrath", takes its title from his first chapter.
Four dated messages over four months in 520 BC, the most precisely dated book in the Bible.
The exiles have been home for years and the Temple is still rubble. Haggai asks why they live in panelled houses.
It worked. Work restarted within a month of his first sermon.

1.t: A Call to Rebuild the Temple

2.t: The Coming Glory of God’s House

Zechariah.eyebrow: Eight visions, and a king on a donkey.
facts: Haggai's contemporary, urging the same rebuilding, but through night visions: horsemen, lampstands, a flying scroll.
The Gospels quote it more than any prophet but Isaiah: the king on a donkey, thirty pieces of silver, the pierced one.
Its last chapters are so different that many think a later prophet's work was joined to his.

9.title: Your king comes to you
9.note: Verse 9: rejoice, your king comes, righteous and victorious, humble and riding on a donkey. Five centuries later a man rode into Jerusalem on one, and the crowd knew exactly which chapter he was quoting.

facts: The name means "my messenger", and may be a title rather than a name.
It is a series of arguments: God states a case, the people object, God answers. Six rounds.
It ends by promising Elijah's return before the great day. The next page is Matthew, and John the Baptist.

3.title: The messenger
3.note: "Behold, I send my messenger", the line Mark opens his Gospel with. Then the refiner's fire, and the only place God says "test me": bring the whole tithe and see if the windows of heaven do not open.

facts: It opens with a family tree, from Abraham to Jesus, because its first question is whether he is the promised king.
Five long teaching blocks, like the five books of Moses, the first of them the Sermon on the Mount.
"So that what was spoken by the prophet might be fulfilled": it says this, or something like it, more than a dozen times.

5.title: The Sermon on the Mount begins
5.note: Blessed are the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the meek. Nine blessings for the people the world does not bless. Then salt, light, and "you have heard it said, but I say to you", six times. It runs to the end of chapter 7.

6.title: Our Father
6.note: The Lord's Prayer, in the middle of instructions about not praying for show. Sixty-some words. Then treasure, the eye, two masters, and the lilies of the field, who do not spin and are dressed better than Solomon.

28.title: Go, therefore
28.note: The tomb, the earthquake, the guards like dead men, and the women running with the news. Then a mountain in Galilee and the last words of the book: all nations, baptize, teach, and I am with you always, to the end of the age.

facts: Sixteen chapters, no birth story, no Sermon on the Mount. It starts with a grown man at the Jordan and runs.
Its favourite word is "immediately", more than forty times. Things happen fast.
Most scholars think it was the first Gospel written, and that Matthew and Luke had it open beside them.

1.title: Immediately
1.note: In one chapter: the Baptist, the baptism, forty days in the wilderness, four fishermen called, a demon cast out, a mother-in-law healed, and a town at the door by sunset. Mark does not stop for breath, and neither does Jesus.

16.title: The empty tomb
16.note: The oldest copies of Mark end at verse 8, with the women running away afraid and saying nothing. The verses after that were added early, by someone who could not leave it there. This translation prints both, so you can see the seam.

1.t: The Mission of John the Baptist
1.n: Mark has no birth story. This is where he starts Jesus, as a grown man walking into a river, and it is the first of three times in this Gospel that a voice calls him Son: here, at the transfiguration, and from a Roman soldier at the cross.

1.t: The Temptation and Preaching of Jesus
1.n: The first thing Jesus says in the earliest Gospel is not a rule or a claim about himself. It is that the waiting is over and God's reign has arrived, and that the response is to turn and trust it. Everything after this is that sentence worked out.

2.n: Jesus tells the paralysed man his sins are forgiven before anyone mentions his legs, and the scribes are right that this is the problem: forgiving sins is God's to do. The healing is offered as the evidence. It is the first open clash of the Gospel, and it is about who he is.

3.n: Twelve, for the twelve tribes. Choosing that number is a claim in itself: Jesus is not gathering followers so much as re-founding Israel around himself, and everyone watching would have heard it that way.

4.n: The parable about parables. Mark puts it first because it explains the rest: the word goes out to everyone the same way, and what happens next depends on the ground it lands on.

4.t: The Parable of the Sower Explained
The Parable of the Mustard Seed

4.n: In the Hebrew scriptures, calming the sea is something God does and nobody else. The disciples' question at the end, asking who this is that even the wind obeys, is the one the whole Gospel is arranging an answer to.

6.t: The Feeding of the Five Thousand
6.n: The only miracle in all four Gospels. The details are deliberate: people sitting in ordered groups on green grass, bread broken and given, twelve baskets left over. Mark is describing a shepherd feeding Israel in the wilderness, and expects you to notice.

7.t: The Faith of the Gentile Woman
7.n: The only person in Mark who argues with Jesus and wins. She is a Gentile, and her line about the crumbs is the hinge: from here the Gospel goes outward, and the feeding that follows happens on the other side of the lake.

8.t: The Feeding of the Four Thousand
The Leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod

8.n: The hinge of the Gospel, and it sits exactly halfway. Everything before it asks who Jesus is; everything after it walks to Jerusalem. Peter gets the answer right and, in the next breath, shows he has understood none of what it costs.

Three times in three chapters Jesus says plainly that he will be killed and rise, and three times the disciples change the subject. Mark builds the whole middle of his book on that gap, and this is the first time he turns and tells the crowd the same road is theirs.

9.n: Moses and Elijah, the law and the prophets, standing with him; then a cloud, and the same voice from the baptism, this time telling the disciples to listen. It comes six days after Peter's confession and it is the answer to it.

9.t: The Boy with an Evil Spirit
The Second Prediction of the Passion

10.t: The Third Prediction of the Passion
The Request of James and John
10.n: The sentence the early church quoted more than almost any other in Mark: that he came to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many. It is the Gospel's own summary of what the cross is for, and it arrives as a correction to two men asking for power.

11.n: He arrives on a donkey, which is the deliberate part: Zechariah had described a king coming that way, humble, rather than on a warhorse. The crowd shouts Hosanna, meaning save us. Within a week the same city calls for his execution.

Not a loss of temper. Overturning the tables in the one place sacrifice could legally happen was an acted parable about the temple's end, and Mark wraps it inside the withered fig tree on purpose. It is what gets him killed: the arrest warrant is issued three verses later.

12.t: The Parable of the Wicked Tenants

12.n: A scribe asks which command outranks the rest, and the answer is two joined together: love God with everything, love your neighbour as yourself. Jesus is quoting Deuteronomy and Leviticus, so nothing here is new. Putting them side by side and calling them the whole of it is.

13.t: The Return of the Son of Man
The Lesson of the Fig Tree

14.n: A Passover meal, which is a meal about being brought out of Egypt, and he hands it a new meaning in the middle. Every Christian communion service in the world is a repetition of this table, and Paul is quoting the words within about twenty years.

The one place the Gospels let you hear him afraid. He asks for the cup to pass and then does not take the offer, and Mark keeps the Aramaic word he used for Father, Abba, because whoever first told the story could not bring themselves to translate it.
Mark cuts between two rooms on purpose. Inside, Jesus finally answers the question of who he is and is condemned for it; outside, in the same hour, Peter says three times that he never knew him.

15.n: Darkness, a cry, and then two things at once: the temple curtain torn from top to bottom, and a Roman officer, the enemy, saying this man was God's Son. Mark has been withholding that confession from every human character for fifteen chapters and finally gives it to a foreigner at an execution.

16.n: The women come to finish a burial and find it undone. In all four Gospels women are the first witnesses, which is not what anyone inventing a story in the first century would have chosen: their testimony did not count in a court.

The oldest copies of Mark stop at verse 8, with the women running away and saying nothing to anyone. What follows was added early by someone who could not leave it there. It is printed here, as in most Bibles, with the seam showing.

facts: A physician, by tradition, and the only Gentile author in the Bible. He wrote Acts too; together they are a quarter of the New Testament.
Only Luke has the annunciation, the manger, the shepherds, the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son.
Women, the poor, Samaritans, tax collectors: the people on the edge are at its centre.

2.title: The birth
2.note: A census, a manger, shepherds in a field, and an army of angels saying peace. The Christmas story as most of the world knows it is this chapter. Its last scene is a twelve-year-old lost in the Temple, and his mother keeping it all in her heart.

15.title: Lost and found
15.note: Three stories with one shape: a sheep, a coin, a son, each lost, each found, each with a party. The third is the longest Jesus ever told, and it ends without an ending: the older brother is still outside, and the father is still pleading.

24.title: The road to Emmaus
24.note: Two disciples walk seven miles with a stranger who explains the whole Old Testament to them, and they do not know him until he breaks bread. "Did not our hearts burn within us?" The book ends where it began, in the Temple.

facts: It begins before Genesis: "In the beginning was the Word." No manger, no parables, no exorcisms.
Seven signs and seven "I am" sayings: the bread, the light, the door, the shepherd, the resurrection, the way, the vine.
It was written, it says, so that you may believe. It is the last Gospel, and reads as if it has thought the longest.

1.title: The Word became flesh
1.note: Eighteen verses of poetry that the church reads at Christmas, then John the Baptist pointing, then two disciples asking where he is staying. "Come and see." By the end of the chapter, Nathanael has been seen under a fig tree.

3.title: Nicodemus
3.note: A teacher of Israel comes at night with a compliment and leaves with a riddle: you must be born again. Verse 16 is here, the most quoted sentence in the Bible. Nicodemus comes back twice more, in daylight, the last time to bury him.

11.title: Lazarus
11.note: Jesus waits two days on purpose, and arrives to a four-day-old grave. "I am the resurrection and the life." Verse 35, "Jesus wept", is the shortest in the English Bible. He raises the dead, and the council decides that he must die.

20.title: Thomas
20.note: Mary in the garden, mistaking him for the gardener until he says her name. Then a locked room, and a week later Thomas, who wanted to touch the wounds. "Blessed are those who have not seen, and have believed." That is you.

facts: Luke's second volume, picking up where his Gospel stopped: the ascension, then the Spirit, then the world.
It follows Peter for twelve chapters and Paul for sixteen, from Jerusalem to Rome.
In several later chapters the narrator says "we". Luke was there.

2.title: Pentecost
2.note: Wind, fire, and fishermen speaking languages they never learned, to pilgrims from fifteen named nations. Peter, who denied him seven weeks earlier, preaches to thousands. Three thousand are baptized before nightfall.

9.title: The road to Damascus
9.note: Saul, who held the coats at Stephen's stoning, is knocked down by light and a question: "why do you persecute me?" Three days blind, then a frightened man named Ananias lays hands on him. The persecutor becomes the missionary.

facts: Written to a church he had never visited, to introduce himself and his Gospel before he arrived.
It is the most systematic thing Paul wrote: sin, faith, grace, Israel, and how to live, in that order.
Augustine, Luther and Wesley each traced their conversion to a sentence in it.

8.title: Nothing can separate us
8.note: The chapter people memorise. No condemnation, the Spirit praying with groans too deep for words, all things working together for good, and the ending: neither death nor life nor anything else in creation can separate us from the love of God.

12.title: A living sacrifice
12.note: After eleven chapters of argument, the turn to practice: present your bodies, do not be conformed, be transformed. One body with many members. Bless those who persecute you. Overcome evil with good.

facts: Corinth was a port with a reputation, and its church had factions, a lawsuit, a scandal, and a fight about the Lord's Supper.
Paul answers their letter point by point: marriage, meat offered to idols, spiritual gifts, the resurrection.
It holds the Bible's most read wedding passage, chapter 13, in the middle of an argument about tongues.

13.title: Love
13.note: Patient, kind, not envious, not boastful, not rude. Read at weddings, but written to a church at war with itself, right after a chapter about spiritual gifts and right before one. "The greatest of these is love."

15.title: The resurrection
15.note: Verses 3 to 7 are the oldest Christian creed, older than any Gospel: died, buried, raised, seen. Then the argument: if Christ is not raised, your faith is worthless. And the seed that must die to become the plant.

2.t: Paul’s Message by the Spirit’s Power

6.t: The Temple of the Holy Spirit

15.t: Where, O Death, Is Your Victory?

facts: The most personal of his letters. He has been attacked, and it shows: he defends himself, boasts, and apologises for boasting.
It lists what he has been through: beaten five times, stoned once, shipwrecked three times, a night and a day adrift.
"My grace is sufficient for you" is here, and the thorn in the flesh that no one has identified.

12.title: The thorn
12.note: Paul tells of being caught up to the third heaven, and then of a thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan, that he asked three times to have removed. The answer: my grace is sufficient, for power is made perfect in weakness.

3.t: The Glory of the New Covenant

facts: Paul is angry. There is no thanksgiving at the start, which every other letter of his has.
The question is whether Gentile converts must be circumcised. His answer is the letter.
He signs off in his own hand, in large letters, and mentions it.

5.title: The fruit of the Spirit
5.note: Freedom, but not for the flesh. The works of the flesh are a list of fifteen; the fruit of the Spirit is singular, one fruit with nine flavours: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control.

facts: Written from prison, and the calmest thing Paul wrote: no crisis, no opponents, only the size of what God has done.
Its first sentence in Greek runs for twelve verses without a full stop.
It ends with the armour of God, written by a man chained to a Roman soldier.

6.title: The armour of God
6.note: Belt, breastplate, shoes, shield, helmet, sword. Paul is looking at the soldier he is chained to. Only one piece is for attack, the sword, and it is the word of God. Then: pray at all times.

facts: Written in chains, and "rejoice" appears in it more than in any other letter.
Philippi was the first church Paul founded in Europe, and the one that kept sending him money.
Chapter 2 holds a hymn older than the letter, on Christ emptying himself, that the first Christians already sang.

2.title: He emptied himself
2.note: Verses 6 to 11 are a hymn the church sang before Paul wrote it down: equal with God, he took the form of a slave and died on a cross, and so every knee will bow. Paul quotes it to settle an argument about humility.

facts: Written to a town Paul had never seen, against a teaching that added angels and rules to Christ.
Its answer is a poem: in him all things were created, and in him all things hold together.
It is the twin of Ephesians, sharing whole sentences, and was carried by the same messenger.

1.title: The image of the invisible God
1.note: Verses 15 to 20: firstborn of all creation, all things made through him and for him, the head of the body, the firstborn from the dead, reconciling everything through the blood of his cross. The whole cosmos, in six verses.

2.t: Absent in Body, Present in Spirit

facts: Most scholars think this is the oldest book in the New Testament, written within twenty years of the crucifixion.
Paul had been driven out of the city after a few weeks and was anxious about the church he left behind.
Its question is what happens to those who die before Christ returns. Its answer is chapter 4.

4.title: Those who are asleep
4.note: Some in the church have died and the rest are grieving as if they are lost. Paul's answer, verses 13 to 18, is the earliest Christian writing on the resurrection of the dead: the Lord will descend, and the dead in Christ rise first. "Comfort one another with these words."

facts: Someone has told the church that the day of the Lord has already come. Paul writes to say it has not.
It has the line that ended up on factory walls: if anyone will not work, neither let him eat.
Three chapters, and he signs it by hand, as a mark against forgeries.
One of three letters to individuals, Timothy and Titus, about how to run a church and choose its leaders.
Timothy was young, often ill, and in charge of the church at Ephesus. Paul tells him to take a little wine.
"The love of money is a root of all kinds of evil" is here, often misquoted without the "a" and the "kinds".

4.t: A Good Servant of Jesus Christ

facts: By tradition the last thing Paul wrote, from a Roman prison, expecting execution.
He asks for his cloak, his books, and above all the parchments, and for Timothy to come before winter.
"I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith."

4.title: I have finished the course
4.note: Preach the word, in season and out. Then the farewell: poured out like a drink offering, the good fight fought, the crown laid up. And the small requests of an old man in a cold cell: come soon, bring the cloak, bring the books.

facts: Titus was Paul's Greek companion, left on Crete to appoint elders in every town.
Paul quotes a Cretan poet against the Cretans and calls the line true, which is a joke he expects Titus to get.
Three chapters on what leaders should be like, and on grace that trains us to say no.
The shortest of Paul's letters, twenty-five verses, to a friend about a runaway slave.
Onesimus, whose name means "useful", fled Philemon, met Paul in prison, and became a Christian. Paul sends him back with this letter.
Paul never says "free him". He says "receive him as you would me", and adds that he knows Philemon will do more than he asks.
No one knows who wrote it. Origen said in the third century that God alone knows, and no one has done better since.
It reads the whole Old Testament as pointing to Christ: the priest greater than Aaron, the sacrifice offered once.
Its call to faith in chapter 11 is a roll of honour, ending with a crowd of witnesses and a race to run.

11.title: By faith
11.note: Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Moses, Rahab, and then names by the handful. Every one "by faith". They died without receiving what was promised, having seen it from far off. Chapter 12 begins: therefore, run.

3.t: Jesus Our Apostle and High Priest

11.t: The Faith of Abel, Enoch, Noah
The Faith of Abraham and Sarah
The Faith of Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph

facts: By tradition, the brother of Jesus, leader of the Jerusalem church, whose knees were said to be calloused like a camel's from prayer.
It is the most practical book in the New Testament: the tongue, the rich, the sick, wisdom, patience.
Luther called it "an epistle of straw" because it says faith without works is dead. The church kept it anyway.

2.title: Faith without works
2.note: A rich man and a poor man walk into your assembly, and you give the rich one the good seat. James is furious. Then the argument with Paul's readers: even demons believe. Show me your faith without works, and I will show you mine by them.

facts: Written to Christians across five provinces of what is now Turkey, facing suspicion and worse from their neighbours.
Its theme is suffering well, as strangers and pilgrims, with Christ's suffering as the pattern.
"Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you."

2.title: Living stones
2.note: You are being built into a house, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people who once were not a people. Then the hard part: submit, endure unjust suffering as he did, who when reviled did not revile in return.

2.t: The Living Stone and Chosen People

facts: A farewell letter: the writer knows his death is near and wants to leave a reminder.
Its second chapter shares most of its material with Jude, one borrowing from the other.
It says Paul's letters contain things hard to understand, which is the Bible commenting on itself.
It never names its author or its readers. It sounds like the Gospel of John, grown old and repeating what matters.
Light and darkness, love and hate, truth and lies. The words are simple and the sentences circle back.
"God is love" is said twice, in chapter 4, and nowhere else in the Bible in those words.

4.title: God is love
4.note: Test the spirits, then the heart of it: love is from God, God is love, and he loved us first, sending his Son. Perfect love casts out fear. Whoever says he loves God and hates his brother is a liar.

facts: One of the two shortest books in the Bible, a single sheet, addressed to "the chosen lady and her children", probably a church.
The writer calls himself only "the elder".
Walk in love, and do not welcome teachers who deny that Christ came in the flesh. That is the whole letter.
The shortest book in the Bible by word count, a note to a man named Gaius about hospitality.
It names a church leader, Diotrephes, who "loves to be first" and throws people out. He is the villain.
It ends the way letters did: I had much to write, but not with ink and pen. I hope to see you soon.
By tradition another brother of Jesus. He calls himself only a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James.
Twenty-five verses, most of them a warning against false teachers, in a rush of Old Testament examples.
It quotes the book of Enoch, which is not in the Bible, and ends with one of its best-loved blessings.
The only book of the Bible that blesses the person who reads it aloud, in its third verse.
John saw it on Patmos, an island prison, and wrote it to seven churches under a hostile empire.
It ends where Genesis began: a tree of life, a river, and God with his people, with no more night.

1.title: The one like a son of man
1.note: John, in exile, hears a voice like a trumpet on the Lord's day and turns to see seven lampstands and, among them, a figure with eyes like fire and a face like the sun. He falls as if dead. "Do not be afraid. I am the first and the last."

21.title: The new Jerusalem
21.note: A new heaven, a new earth, and a city coming down like a bride. God will wipe away every tear; no more death, mourning, crying or pain. No temple, because God is its temple. Its gates are never shut, because there is no night.
